title: EEG Based Classification of Attentive and Distracted States During Video Based Learning

abstract: Monitoring learner attention during video-based learning is important for adaptive educational systems. However, common indicators such as clicks, video completion, and quiz scores do not directly reflect whether learners remain attentive. Electroencephalography (EEG) provides a noninvasive and time-sensitive measure of brain activity for attention-state assessment. This study investigates whether interpretable EEG spectral features can classify attentive and distracted states during instructional video viewing. EEG recordings from 30 participants in Experiment 2 of the Brain, Body, and Behavior Dataset (BBBD) were analyzed using the common stimulus stim01 under attentive and distracted conditions. The signals were segmented into 4 s windows with 2 s overlap, producing 5278 windows (2730 attentive, 2548 distracted). For each window, 15 EEG features were extracted from delta, theta, alpha, and beta band powers across frontal, parietal, and occipital regions, together with theta/alpha ratios. Four machine learning models SVM, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and XGBoost were evaluated using subjectindependent Leave-One-Subject-Out cross-validation. SVM achieved the best performance, with mean accuracy of 0.6027 and weighted $\mathbf{F 1}$-score of 0.5669. The results show that attentive windows were classified more successfully than distracted windows, suggesting that distraction is harder to detect with the current feature set. These findings provide a stronger benchmark for EEG-based attention classification in video-based learning under subject-independent evaluation.
